subject: history_social
passage: In 2021, a sports academy in Karachi, Pakistan, began offering free cricket coaching to girls on weekend mornings. The academy had long trained mostly boys, and its boys' program continued alongside the new one. Each year, the academy recorded how many boys and girls were enrolled. Coach Sana Baig claims that girls now make up a much larger proportion of the academy's players than they did when the girls' program began.

data.title: Players Enrolled at a Karachi Cricket Academy, 2021-2025

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Baig's claim?

choices.A: The number of boys enrolled at the academy was higher in 2025 than in 2021.
choices.B: More girls than boys were enrolled at the academy in 2025.
choices.C: Girls were about 12% of players in 2021 but about 38% in 2025.
choices.D: The academy enrolled 118 girls in 2025, more than in any other year shown.

explanation.why: Baig's claim is about proportion: the share of all players who are girls. A rising number of girls alone does not prove this, since the number of boys could rise too. In 2021 girls were 24 of 204 players (about 12%), and in 2025 they were 118 of 314 (about 38%).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (196 versus 180), but it is about boys and does not show the girls' share growing.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This misreads the table: in 2025 there were 196 boys and only 118 girls.
explanation.C: Correct. The girls' share of all players roughly tripled, from about 12% to about 38%, which directly supports a claim about proportion.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it gives only a number of girls, not their share of all players, so it cannot show that the proportion grew.
